title: Pharmaceutical Sample Management — Operational Lifecycle
summary: The nine-step operational lifecycle for pharmaceutical sample management in a commercial CRM, covering the end-to-end flow from lot creation through field distribution to reconciliation and auditing.

findings.nine_step_lifecycle: Step 1: Lot Creation — sample lots are registered with product, quantity, expiration date, and regulatory classification. Step 2: Shipment — lots are allocated and shipped to field representatives with chain-of-custody documentation. Step 3: Receipt and Acknowledgement — field representatives confirm receipt, triggering inventory initialization in their local stock. Step 4: Inventory Counting — periodic physical counts reconcile system records against actual stock. Step 5: Distribution — samples are disbursed to healthcare providers with electronic signature capture at the point of delivery. Step 6: Transfer — samples move between representatives through documented transfer-in and transfer-out transactions. Step 7: Return — unused or expired samples are returned through a documented return process. Step 8: Adjustment — discrepancies are resolved through adjustment transactions with mandatory reason codes. Step 9: Reconciliation and Audit — comprehensive reconciliation of all transactions to ensure a complete chain of custody from receipt through final disposition.
findings.regulatory_drivers: The lifecycle is designed to satisfy PDMA (Prescription Drug Marketing Act, 21 CFR Part 203) requirements for sample distribution record-keeping, signature capture, and reconciliation. Controlled substances add 21 CFR 1300-1316 requirements for additional tracking and reporting.
findings.signature_capture: Electronic signatures are captured at the point of sample delivery on mobile devices. Signatures become read-only after acceptance, are cryptographically bound to the transaction record, and satisfy 21 CFR Part 11 requirements for electronic signatures. Signature data includes the signer identity, timestamp, and the specific products and quantities distributed.
findings.inventory_integrity: The system maintains a running inventory balance for each representative, updated in real-time as distribution, transfer, return, and adjustment transactions occur. Physical count workflows detect discrepancies and require documented resolution before the reconciliation cycle closes.

title: Sample Management — Regulatory Framework Deep Dive
summary: Detailed regulatory requirements for pharmaceutical sample management across US federal (PDMA), state, and international jurisdictions, including limit management, DEA scheduling, and CFR Part 11 compliance.

findings.pdma_core_requirements: The Prescription Drug Marketing Act (PDMA, 21 CFR Part 203) establishes federal requirements for sample distribution in the US. Key mandates: (1) Samples may only be distributed to licensed practitioners who submit a written request, (2) Every sample transaction must be documented with product name, quantity, lot number, date, and recipient identity, (3) Manufacturers must conduct annual physical inventories of sample stock, (4) Representatives must reconcile sample inventories quarterly or upon any change in employment, (5) All records must be retained for at least 3 years, (6) Manufacturers must report significant losses or thefts to FDA within 5 days of discovery.
findings.sample_limits_and_caps: Sample limit management operates at multiple levels: (1) Per-HCP limits — configurable maximum quantity per product per HCP over a rolling period (commonly 12 months). Limits prevent over-distribution and ensure fair access. (2) Per-representative allocation — total sample budget allocated to each rep, tracked against shipments and distributions. (3) Product-level caps — total distribution ceiling per product set by medical affairs or regulatory, enforced across all reps. (4) Customer-specific overrides — some accounts may have negotiated limits higher or lower than defaults. The limit calculation engine evaluates against the rolling period at each distribution attempt and blocks transactions that would exceed the configured maximum.
findings.dea_controlled_substances: Samples of DEA-scheduled substances (Schedules II-V under 21 CFR Parts 1300-1316) require additional controls: (1) Schedule II samples may not be distributed at all — only starter packs under specific conditions, (2) Schedule III-V samples require DEA registration of the distributing entity, (3) Perpetual inventory tracking with no tolerance for discrepancies, (4) Loss/theft reporting to DEA within one business day, (5) Biennial inventory reconciliation, (6) Chain-of-custody documentation at every transfer point. The CRM must flag controlled substance products and enforce these additional workflows automatically.
findings.cfr_part_11_electronic_signatures: 21 CFR Part 11 governs electronic records and signatures in FDA-regulated industries. For sample management: (1) Electronic signatures must be unique to each individual and not reused, (2) Signature records must include the printed name of the signer, date/time of signing, and meaning of the signature (e.g., receipt acknowledgement), (3) Systems must employ controls to ensure the signer's identity, such as PIN plus biometric or two distinct identification components, (4) Signed records must be protected against modification — once captured, the signature and its associated transaction become immutable, (5) Audit trails must record who, what, when, and why for any changes to regulated records.
findings.state_and_local_requirements: Beyond federal PDMA, individual US states may impose additional sample requirements: (1) Some states require sample receipt tracking at the practice/facility level in addition to the individual HCP, (2) Certain states mandate specific reporting of sample distribution data to state pharmacy boards, (3) State licensure verification may be required before distribution — the CRM should integrate with state licensing databases where available. Pharmaceutical companies must configure their sample management system to enforce the most restrictive applicable requirement at each distribution point.
findings.international_variations: Sample regulations vary significantly by country: (1) EU — each member state has its own rules; Germany limits to one smallest pack per product per HCP per visit, max two per year; France requires declaration to ANSM. (2) Japan — samples are 'trial-use drugs' under Pharmaceutical Affairs Act with MHLW reporting requirements. (3) Brazil — ANVISA regulations restrict sample distribution channels and require specific labeling. (4) Many markets prohibit sampling entirely for certain drug categories. Migration projects must map source system sample configurations to the target platform's limit management capabilities on a per-country basis.

title: Sample Management — Migration Considerations and Gotchas
summary: Practical migration challenges, data mapping considerations, and common pitfalls when moving sample management from a legacy CRM to the target platform.

findings.data_migration_scope: Sample management migration involves: (1) Product catalog — all sample-eligible products with lot information, DEA schedule classification, and active/inactive status, (2) Inventory snapshots — current rep inventory balances as of migration cutover, (3) Transaction history — at minimum the current reconciliation period's transactions; many companies migrate 2-3 years for audit trail continuity, (4) Sample limit configurations — per-product, per-HCP, per-territory limits, (5) HCP eligibility — licensure status, sample request records, and opt-out flags, (6) Signature records — historical signatures may be migrated as attachments or archived separately depending on audit requirements.
findings.common_migration_gotchas: Gotcha 1: Inventory balance drift — if the cutover period spans active sampling days, reps may distribute samples between the data extract and go-live, creating inventory mismatches. Freeze sampling 24-48 hours before cutover or perform a delta reconciliation. Gotcha 2: Signature image format — legacy systems may store signatures as proprietary binary formats that must be converted to standard image formats (PNG/JPEG) for the target platform. Gotcha 3: Lot expiration — expired lots in the source system should be migrated as inactive/expired, not filtered out, to maintain the complete audit trail. Gotcha 4: Country-specific limit rules — the source system may enforce limits through custom code rather than configuration; these rules must be explicitly captured and recreated in the target platform's limit management framework. Gotcha 5: Orphaned transactions — transactions referencing deleted products, deactivated reps, or reassigned territories in the source system need a mapping strategy.
findings.parallel_run_recommendation: For regulated sample management, a parallel run of 1-2 reconciliation cycles on both systems is considered a standard practice. This validates that: (1) Inventory balances match between systems, (2) Distribution workflows capture all required regulatory data, (3) Signature capture meets CFR Part 11 requirements in the new system, (4) Limit enforcement produces the same outcomes, (5) Reconciliation reports generate equivalent output for compliance review.
